This guide builds on [Equivalence Classes](equivalence-classes.qmd) and [Causal
Identification](causal-identification.qmd) and covers causal adjustment when the
graph is known only as a PAG, i.e. when the underlying MAG is identified only up
to Markov equivalence.

```{r}
#| label: setup

library(CausalStructures)
```

## Adjustment with a PAG

Consider the MAG from [Equivalence Classes](equivalence-classes.qmd), where `A`
and `B` share a hidden common cause, and `C` and `B` each cause their successor,
with an added direct effect `A --> D`:

```{r}
#| fig-height: 3

mag <- cgraph(A %<->% B, C %-->% B %-->% D, A %-->% D, class = "MAG")
pag <- mag_to_pag(mag)
plot(pag)
```

The resulting PAG contains the circle-marked edge `A o-> B`. Depending on which
MAG in the equivalence class is the true graph, this edge can correspond to
either `A --> B` or `A <-> B`.

Consequently, `backdoor_set()` cannot determine an adjustment set from the PAG
alone:

```{r}
is.null(backdoor_set(pag, "A", "D"))
```

In particular, whether `B` needs to be included in an adjustment set depends on
how the circle at `A` is resolved.

Not every effect here is uncertain. For the effect of `B` on `D`, the PAG admits
an adjustment set that is valid for every MAG in the equivalence class. The
generalized adjustment criterion (GAC) can therefore be applied directly to the
PAG with `all_adjustment_sets()`:

```{r}
all_adjustment_sets(pag, "B", "D", minimal = FALSE)
```

## Adjustment sets

`pagcauses()` considers MAGs compatible with the PAG and returns adjustment sets
that are valid in at least one such MAG [@wang2025pagcauses]:

```{r}
pagcauses(pag, "A", "D")
```

For this example, the empty set is valid when `A --> B`, since there is then no
backdoor path from `A` to `D` through `B`. When `A <-> B`, `B` must instead be
included to block the path through the hidden common cause. Thus `{B}` is a
valid adjustment set in that case; nonminimal supersets such as `{B, C}` may
also be returned when they are valid.

The same procedure applies when the ambiguity occurs elsewhere in the graph. For
example:

```{r}
pagcauses(pag, "C", "D")
```

If there is no MAG compatible with the PAG in which `D` can have a causal effect
on `A`, `pagcauses()` returns no possible causal effect:

```{r}
pagcauses(pag, "D", "A")
```

This is consistent with `possible_ancestors()`.

::: {.callout-note title="No selection bias"}
`pagcauses()`, `possible_local_structures()`, and `maximal_local_mag()` assume
that the PAG has no selection bias, matching the assumptions in the source
papers. Selection bias shows up as an undirected edge in a PAG, and all three
functions throw an error if the PAG has one:

```{r}
#| error: true

selection_pag <- cgraph(A %---% B %---% C %---% D %---% A, class = "PAG")
pagcauses(selection_pag, "A", "B")
```
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Why not just enumerate the MAGs?"}
One could enumerate all MAGs with `enumerate_mags()` and apply `backdoor_set()`
to each one. However, the number of MAGs in a Markov equivalence class grows as
$O(3^{(d^2-d)/2})$ with the number of nodes $d$.

`pagcauses()` avoids constructing these MAGs. Instead, it uses graphical
conditions to check whether a candidate adjustment set can be valid for a MAG
compatible with the PAG. This reduces the complexity to $O(5^d d^6)$
[@wang2025pagcauses, Section 3.4].

Depending on your graph size, the brute force approach could of course still be
faster in practice.
:::

## Local structures

`pagcauses()` builds on a smaller graphical primitive:
`possible_local_structures()`. For a single node `x`, this function enumerates
which subsets of its circle-marked neighbors could resolve to `x <-> v`, with
the remaining circle-marked edges resolving to `x --> v`, in some consistent
MAG [@wang2023localbk]:

```{r}
possible_local_structures(pag, "A")
```

`A` has one circle-marked neighbor, `B`, so there are two local structures: the
empty set, corresponding to `A --> B`, and `{B}`, corresponding to `A <-> B`.
Pairing a local structure with `maximal_local_mag()` resolves the edges around
`A` implied by this local background knowledge:

```{r}
maximal_local_mag(pag, "A", character())
```

```{r}
maximal_local_mag(pag, "A", "B")
```

These correspond to the two cases considered by `pagcauses(pag, "A", "D")`: the
first gives `{}` as a valid adjustment set for `A` and `D`, while the second
gives `{B}`. The result is returned as an `UNKNOWN` graph rather than a MAG,
since local background knowledge about one node need not resolve every circle in
the graph.
